title: A wedding song at a funeral
hookLine: Sohila is also sung at cremations, a song of the soul going home

lines: THE SAME FIVE HYMNS AS LAST NIGHT.
cards: A first-dance song at a graveside would stop a room cold.

Yet at a Sikh cremation, once the fire is lit, the words recited sound, to anyone who knows them, like a wedding: the date written, oil poured at the threshold, friends asked for their blessings, a bride called to meet her Lord.
It's Sohila, the same five hymns said at bedtime. Here the wedding words aren't a mistake. They're the point.

teach.h: THE PYRE IS LIT; SOHILA IS SUNG.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets out the funeral. The body is washed and dressed, and the family gathers.

At the cremation ground, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila, and then the Ardas is said. In the days that follow, a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib is begun, at home or at a gurdwara.
Sikh teaching also asks mourners not to give way to loud wailing. Grief is real, and tears are human, but the songs are of praise. So why Sohila?
Go back to its first hymn. The date has been written. Friends, pour the oil, give your blessings, so I may meet my Lord.
The summons goes to every house, every day.

teach.h: THE SUMMONS ARRIVES FOR ONE SOUL.
teach.b: Read at the pyre, the funeral becomes the day that summons arrives for one soul, and the wedding is the meeting with the Beloved. In the hymn's language, the person who has died isn't lost to darkness.
They're going home, the way a bride goes to her new home.
And if the same five hymns are sung at bedtime and at the end of a life, some readers hear every night as a small rehearsal: lying down, letting go of the day, trusting the morning to the One.
The last line of Sohila, sung at the pyre as at the pillow, is Guru Arjan asking to be the dust of the holy's feet. Even at the end, humility.

how: At a Sikh cremation, once the pyre is lit, the sangat recites Kirtan Sohila and then the Ardas, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada directs; the same hymns are said by Sikhs every night before sleep.

games.why: the Rehat Maryada directs that Sohila be recited at the pyre, then the Ardas: the night song becomes the song of going home.

practice: Let one person who has died come to mind, a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, and picture their face on a good day, with one kindness, one habit, one laugh of theirs. If grief comes, let it come; nothing needs fixing.
Hold them like a friend at the door wishing a traveler well, and if you pray, say Waheguru for them, softly.

wordCard.voice: Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct that sets out the funeral: Kirtan Sohila is sung there as well as at bedtime, the soul as a bride, called to meet the Beloved and going home.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sohila, a song of praise and joy; sung at bedtime and at the cremation ground.
